alsoUsed.example: I added a 5 GB data bolt-on to my phone plan for the trip.
alsoUsed.meaning: (bolt-on, noun, mainly British) an optional extra you can add to a basic package, such as extra mobile data

deep.atWork: We can bolt the new authentication layer onto your existing system, but a proper redesign would be more secure in the long term.

confusedWith.difference: Integrate means to combine parts so they work together as one whole; bolt on means to add a part on the outside, often without deep integration.
Add is neutral and general; bolt on suggests the addition is separate, attached to something already built, and often a quick fix.
This is a different meaning: to run off suddenly, as in 'The horse bolted', unrelated to attaching things.

contexts.sentence: The new wing had clearly been bolted onto the old house as an afterthought, and it never quite matched the original stone.
Rather than rebuild the platform, we propose to bolt a reporting module onto the current system.
Their new app just feels like they bolted a chat feature onto it because everyone else has one.

deep.register: Informal to neutral; common in business, tech, and journalism, and used figuratively. It would be out of place in very formal or legal writing, where 'incorporate' or 'integrate' is safer, and it can sound dismissive if you want to praise a well-planned integration.
deep.summary: To bolt something onto something is to attach a new feature, technology, or process to an existing system as an extra part, instead of rebuilding or redesigning the whole thing. The image comes from physically fastening a separate piece onto a structure with a bolt, so the new part sits on the outside and stays distinct from the original. It often carries a slightly critical feeling: the addition is quick or convenient but may be awkward, superficial, or not fully integrated.

example: Existing factories do bolt AI onto old layouts.
example2: We don't want a bolt-on AI tool; we want it built into the planning process.
knownAs: a metal fastener, or to run away suddenly ("the horse bolted")
meaning: to add something to an existing system as an extra part, without redesigning the whole thing
pattern: bolt something onto something · bolt-on (adj.), e.g. a bolt-on solution
situation: From a Cowork chat about Scene & Say, 8 Oct: you met it in "Existing factories do bolt AI onto old layouts" and hadn't seen this use before.
usage: Business and tech writing; often a mild criticism of a quick, surface-level fix. The opposite is to build something in or integrate it.
